newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: P.W. Botha ordered bombing, S.African court hears.
newsitem.headline: P.W. Botha ordered bombing, S.African court hears.

text.p: Former South African president P.W. Botha was dragged deeper on Tuesday into accusations that he knew a great deal about the apartheid regime's dirty tricks against opponents -- and even ordered a civilian bombing.

Convicted state assassin Eugene de Kock said in a Pretoria court that his superiors had told him Botha directly ordered the bombing of the Johannesburg headquarters of the black trade union federation Cosatu in the late 1980s.

The former death squad leader de Kock, testifying in the hope of winning leniency for the six murders and scores of other charges he was convicted of last month, said he had asked his security boss at the time who ordered the Cosatu House bombing.
"From the highest was the reply and I said 'from where, the state president?' and he said 'yes'," he told the court.

The bespectacled De Kock, wearing a grey suit, also admitted he was part of a South African group that flew to London in the 1980s to blow up the headquarters of Nelson Mandela's exiled African National Congress liberation movement.
Suspicious Heathrow airport police had interrogated him for five hours but let him go, and he was relaxing on a flight home when the explosives went off.

On Monday de Kock said Botha, who yielded to reformer F.W. de Klerk in 1989, must have known about a South African agents' attack he led into neighbouring Lesotho on suspected ANC members in which some 10 people died in 1985.
"I have no doubt state president P.W. Botha knew about it," he told the hushed court, where even ANC cabinet ministers have come to hear his revelations.
Botha has remained silent on these and earlier accusations, saying simply he has nothing to apologise for.
De Kock, hoping to escape a life sentence, has vowed to name his superiors in the highest ranks in order to prove that the ghastly crimes he committed were done according to orders.
He also named apartheid-era foreign minister Pik Botha, police chief Adriaan Vlok and numerous police and army generals as figures who must have known about the cross-border raids.

De Kock has begun to lift the lid on numerous killings of anti-apartheid activists, many of which he carried out himself during 30 years as a policeman, including a stint as head of the notorious Vlakplaas death squad unit in the 1980s.

P.W. Botha, who says he started the reforms that under de Klerk led to black majority rule in 1994 after three centuries of white supremacy, is now a frail 80-year-old and lives quietly with his wife at a retirement home by the sea.

De Klerk has blamed the state of emergency that Botha imposed in the 1980s for creating an atmosphere ripe for many of the human rights abuses that Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth and reconciliation commission is trying to exorcise.
De Kock, 47, has applied to the commission for an amnesty. This will depend partly on how frank he is in telling the dark secrets he knows.
But Botha, rarely seen now in public, said last year he would not help Tutu's work or apologise for anything.
"I am not going to the truth commission. I am not going to repent. I am not going to ask for favours," he said.
"What I did, I did for my country, for my God, for my people and for all the people of South Africa."
